blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes the paper 'Certificate Transparency' by Ben Laurie, which introduces the concept of a publicly verifiable append-only log to build trust in Certificate Authorities (CAs) without relying on blockchain. The core idea is a cryptographically verifiable log of all issued certificates, enabling clients and servers to detect misissued certificates. Laurie critiques Bitcoin and blockchain-based alternatives like DNSChain, highlighting their inefficiency and lack of verification mechanisms. The paper details how to construct such a log using Merkle trees, anti-entropy protocols, and eventual consistency models, with a dynamic approach to the number of logs based on certificate lifetime. The author also explores broader applications, such as 'Binary Transparency,' which could create trusted registries for software binaries like Docker images, making targeted malware deployment harder.
paper_abstract:
Why Provable Transparency is Useful Against Surveillance
Ben Laurie, Google (benl@google,com), 11 Jan 2014.

Background
Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962) is an example of a general mechanism which permits a
public, verifiable, append­only log of stuff.
In the case of CT, the stuff is X.509v3 certificates, but it works equally well for anything that can be
expressed as bits.
Verifiable append­only logs can also be used to create verifiable maps1 .
